title: EC-Council ECIH
summary: The EC-Council Certified Incident Handler (ECIH, exam code ECIH) is an intermediate-level certification for security analysts who deal with live incidents. It suits SOC analysts, help desk engineers moving into security operations, and administrators who must contain a breach before it spreads. It proves to an employer that you can follow a recognised incident handling process, from preparation through containment, eradication and recovery to lessons learned. The exam is a knowledge test of multiple choice questions with scenario items, sat at a testing centre or online with a proctor. It leads to incident response analyst, SOC analyst and incident handler roles. Check EC-Council's current exam blueprint before booking, because the domain list below follows the published objectives and is revised from time to time. This is an independent study guide and it is not affiliated with EC-Council.

beginner.definition: The ECIH is a certification from EC-Council about incident handling. Incident handling means the steps you follow when a company is attacked or a system breaks its security rules. The exam tests whether you know how to prepare for attacks and how to respond when they happen. It sits between entry level training and specialist forensics work.
beginner.whyItMatters: Every company needs people who stay calm when a security alarm fires. This certification shows an employer that you understand a structured response process and not just a list of tools. It helps you move from a support desk role into a security operations centre. It also gives you a shared language for working with managers and lawyers during a real breach. The exam is well known, so recruiters recognise it on a CV.
howItWorks: Start by learning the vocabulary. Learn what an event, an incident and a breach mean, because the exam uses these words precisely.
Study the incident handling lifecycle as a loop. It runs from preparation through identification, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned.
Work through the attack categories in the syllabus. They include malware, email attacks, web attacks and network attacks.
Practise on a home lab. Follow a written runbook and write a short incident report for each exercise you finish.
Review the official exam blueprint. Book the exam when your practice scores are steady rather than lucky.
The exam itself is a proctored knowledge test. It uses multiple choice questions, including scenario items about a described incident.
beginner.example: Picture a finance team member who opens an email attachment at nine in the morning. By lunchtime, files on a shared drive are renamed. A pop up on the screen then demands payment. An incident handler does not simply delete the email. First they confirm what happened. Next they stop the spread by isolating the machine and remove the harmful software. Then they restore clean files from backup. Finally they write down what worked, so the next case is faster. That ordered thinking is what the ECIH exam measures.
takeaways: Learn the vocabulary first, because the exam grades precise wording.
Write a practice runbook and an incident report, not just study notes.
Check the current EC-Council blueprint before you book a date.

objectives: Explain the difference between a security event, an incident and a breach using the words correctly.
Describe the incident handling lifecycle and the activities performed at each stage.
Identify the common attack categories that cause incidents and the evidence each one leaves behind.
Outline the first response steps for a malware, email, web or network incident.
Describe how to preserve evidence so that later investigation stays trustworthy.
Produce a short incident report that states impact, actions taken and lessons learned.

chapters.title: Introduction to Incident Handling and Response
objectives: Distinguish between an event, an incident and a breach, and explain why the difference changes the response.
Describe the roles inside an incident response team and what each role owns during a live case.
Outline the phases of the incident handling lifecycle from preparation to lessons learned.
Explain how standards such as the NIST incident handling guidance shape an organisation's process.
List the information an incident handler must record when a case is first opened.

chapters.title: Attacker Frameworks and the Incident Handling Lifecycle
objectives: Explain the stages of the Cyber Kill Chain and what defenders can observe at each stage.
Use the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base to map observed activity to known techniques.
Describe how the incident handling process connects to the attacker stages in these frameworks.
Identify which defensive control can break an attack chain at a chosen stage.
Explain how threat intelligence feeds into detection and response decisions.

chapters.title: Incident Response and Handling Procedures
objectives: Describe the containment options for a compromised host and the trade offs of each choice.
Explain how to eradicate malicious code, persistence and unauthorised accounts from a system.
Describe how to restore services from a trusted backup and confirm they are clean.
Apply the order of volatility when deciding what evidence to collect first.
Write an incident report that records impact, actions, evidence and lessons learned.

chapters.title: Handling Malware Incidents
objectives: Identify the main malware families and the symptoms each one produces on a host.
Describe the safe steps for triaging a suspected infected machine before cleaning it.
Explain how to check for persistence mechanisms such as scheduled tasks and startup entries.
Describe how to confirm that a cleaned system stays clean after it returns to the network.

chapters.title: Handling Email Incidents
objectives: Analyse email headers to trace the real sender and the route a message travelled.
Recognise the signs of phishing, spoofing and business email compromise in a reported message.
Describe how to search a mail system for all copies of a malicious message and remove them.
Explain the containment steps for a user who already clicked a link or opened an attachment.
Describe how to brief users after an email incident so that reporting improves.

chapters.title: Handling Network Incidents
objectives: Identify the signs of denial of service, man in the middle and network scanning activity.
Describe how to use flow records and packet captures to confirm what crossed the network.
Explain the containment options for a network incident, such as blocking a port or an address.
Describe the response steps for an incident involving a network device such as a router or switch.
Explain how to verify that normal network behaviour has returned after containment.

chapters.title: Handling Web Application and Server Incidents
objectives: Recognise common web attack patterns such as injection, cross site scripting and file upload abuse.
Read web server and application logs to find the requests linked to an incident.
Describe the containment steps for a compromised web server while keeping evidence intact.
Explain how to check a web application for the vulnerabilities an attacker used.
Describe how to verify that defaced or altered content has been fully removed.

chapters.title: Forensic Readiness and Incident Reporting
objectives: Explain why logging, clock synchronisation and retention settings decide what an investigation can prove.
Describe how to collect volatile and non volatile evidence without altering it.
Maintain a chain of custody record for every item of evidence you handle.
Explain how the lessons learned review turns one incident into better detection rules.
Present incident findings to a non technical audience in plain language.
